summary:
We built Anvis, a web tool that lets anyone watch a patch of the infrared sky change over time using NASA’s SPHEREx data. Users enter a position (RA and Dec) or click one of the five challenge targets. Anvis finds every SPHEREx image of that spot in NASA’s IRSA archive, downloads small cutouts, removes the zodiacal-light background, aligns the frames to one north-up grid and plays them as a flip-book.

To help spot movers, it offers Blink and Difference modes, stacked images for each survey visit, Gaia DR3 and WISE overlays moved to each frame’s date, a light curve, plain-word quality flags and a shareable link. New data releases are added by changing one setting.

This matters because SPHEREx has imaged over a billion objects, too many to check by hand, and most known comets and brown dwarfs were found by people comparing images over time. Anvis removes the coding barrier, so students and volunteers can make that comparison in a browser.
details:
What it does and how it works
Anvis is a web tool for watching a patch of the infrared sky change over time. You enter RA and Dec, or click one of the five challenge targets. The Python backend finds every SPHEREx image of that spot in NASA’s IRSA archive and downloads only a small cutout of each. It subtracts the zodiacal-light background, reads the wavelength and quality flags, and lines all the frames up on one north-up grid. The browser then plays them as a flip-book. A user can also switch to Blink or Difference mode, stack the frames of each survey visit into one cleaner image, overlay Gaia DR3 and WISE sources, plot a light curve, and share the exact view as a link.

Benefits and intended impact
Moving and changing objects are hard to find because the data is huge and the raw files are hard to use. Anvis lets students, volunteers and researchers do that comparison in a browser, with no coding. We hope it helps more people spot candidate movers such as brown dwarfs, asteroids, comets and variable stars.

Tools used

  • Python, Flask and Gunicorn for the backend
  • Astropy and NumPy for FITS files, sky coordinates and resampling
  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with HTML5 Canvas for the interface
  • NASA IRSA (SPHEREx images, WISE catalogues) and MAST (Gaia DR3)
  • Docker and a Procfile for deployment
  • pytest, with 118 offline tests that don’t need the internet, plus browser tests for the interface
  • Claude for development and debugging, and Gemini for research
  • No special hardware, only normal computers

What is creative

  • Stacked images for each survey visit, weighted by their noise
  • Difference images shown in units of noise, so constant stars cancel and a mover leaves a yellow and blue pair
  • Gaia and WISE positions moved to each frame’s date, so a source with a WISE match but no Gaia match is flagged as a brown-dwarf candidate
  • A light curve, plus quality flags shown in plain words

What we considered

  • Honest science: wavelength changes across each detector, so we show it on every frame, and we label saturated stars as relative measurements.
  • Being kind to NASA’s servers: limited parallel requests, retries with waiting time, caching, and small downloads.
  • Easy updates: a new SPHEREx release is added by changing one setting.
  • Clear credit: the page says it is an independent tool and not an official NASA site.
